method: Read the spec at 78e35627 in full and the lap-1 outcomes in docs/decisions/decision-changelog.md. Traced the open path in the app: web/app/play/OpenFileControl.tsx (accept), web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx (runRequestNotation, requestNotation, acceptDropped, the shell's score-loaded handler, the header props), web/app/play/NotationSurface.tsx (the render effect and the re-assert guard), web/app/play/TracksPopover.tsx (its guard), web/lib/alphatab/useAlphaTab.ts (how listeners subscribe) and web/e2e/player.e2e.ts (openFirstScore, the late-sample test). Traced AlphaTab 1.8.4's dist: EventEmitterOfT, renderScore, _internalRenderTracks, _onScoreLoaded, the facade's settings.core.file load, ScoreLoader.loadScoreAsync and the Score type. Traced Sentry 11.0.0's tag path in the source mirror (prepareEvent, Scope.update and clone, the scope-data merge, envelope serialization; the twelve core files on the capture path are identical to the 11.0.0 tag on GitHub), Sentry's search grammar (getsentry/sentry:src/sentry/api/event_search.py), Relay's tag limits (getsentry/relay tags.rs and trimming.rs) and Sentry's public docs on tags, search and issue details. Ran: the quote check (27 of 27 verbatim); a Node script that parses every fixture and bundled file with the installed AlphaTab and prints the tag under the current format and with 3-digit padding, plus wildcard over-match and length counts; a Node script that drives the installed AlphaTabApiBase through the late bundled-sample race with listeners in the app's order; a Node script with the installed React 19.2.7 and jsdom that measures when an E105 is reported against when the render effect runs; and F-23 option 1 end to end through Sentry 11.0.0's captureException, built from the mirror with the repo's installed esbuild. Every draft below was applied to a scratch copy of the spec and passed the repo's Prettier, markdownlint and cspell configurations, with no line over 100 characters.

after_draft.text:
- `web/app/play/OpenFileControl.tsx` and `web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx`, beyond their catch sites:
  picking or dropping a file remembers its name (3.2) and clears the `instruments` tag (2.3);
  `requestNotation` remembers the score's names as soon as the file parses (3.2); the score-loaded
  handler sets the tag; `readNotation` and `LoadedNotation` carry the file's extension (2.3).

- **E105 keeps its message.** It is our own code failing after the file was read, so the message
  describes our bug, not the file. The names filter (section 3.2) still runs over it, and it already
  holds the new score's names: they are remembered as soon as the file parses.

- **Remembered as soon as a file parses.** `requestNotation` calls `rememberScore` right after
  `loadScoreFromBytes` returns, before the new score replaces the open one. Two reports can be sent
  before AlphaTab's score-loaded event: an E105 thrown after the parse, and a crash while the header
  draws the new title (E901). Both keep their message, so the names must be on the list by then.

items.scenario: You open `Punk.gp` on `/play`. A future bug in our open code throws right after the file parses, with the message `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'Distortion Guitar')`, and you see E105. The report reaches Sentry with `Distortion Guitar` still in it, because the names list learns the score's track names only when AlphaTab draws the score, after the report has gone.
items.corrections: (1) E105's window starts at the read flag, not at the parse: a throw in the engine wait, the replace prompt or the frame wait before the parse is an E105 too, but then the score has no names yet and the file name was already remembered at the pick. The gap that matters runs from PlayerShell.tsx:871 returning to NotationSurface's effect. (2) 'Keep the score-loaded call for the bundled sample' protects nothing: the sample is the app's own file (web/public/notation/1-beat.gp has no title and one track named `Drums`). Keeping that call is harmless; the drafts drop it as simpler. (3) The proposed test cannot sit in the OpenFileControl test, which replaces onNotation with a stub; it belongs in web/app/play/PlayerShell.test.tsx, which already renders the real shell with the real engine namespace. (4) Place the call after the parse's own try/catch (PlayerShell.tsx:870-889), so a throw from rememberScore itself is reported as E105, not as the visitor's E103.
items.notes_for_triage:
How F-21, F-22, F-23 and F-25 interact: all four are about work the spec puts in AlphaTab's score-loaded handler, and each moves or limits it. F-21 moves rememberScore to the parse in requestNotation. F-25 moves the tag to the moment an opened file replaces the open score; that makes F-22's fix unnecessary (no handler reads the late sample's event), and the handler is left with nothing to do for monitoring. F-23 option 1 then never clears the tag and removes it only from the reports of a failed open. Together they need no listener order, no ref and no restore path. F-23 option 2 does not fit F-25's placement: after an E105 thrown once the swap is queued, its catch would put back the old score's tag over the new score, and no later event would correct it. One more reason to keep monitoring code out of that handler: during the bundled sample's load, AlphaTab's own loader catches any throw from a score-loaded listener (@coderline/alphatab@1.8.4:dist/alphaTab.core.mjs:30186-30192) and raises it as its error event, so a bug there would show the E202 banner 'The player engine could not start'.

Combined wording if all four are applied (F-21; F-22; F-23 option 1; F-25). Up to 'the number is enough.' the §2.3 bullet is the current text, so F-24 can still edit that part on its own. With this wording, §6 also changes: drop 'and picking a file clears the `instruments` tag before the file is read' (lines 468-469), add F-23 option 1's reportError case (line 453) and F-21's PlayerShell case, and optionally hold the sample back in case 4 (F-22).

  picking or dropping a file remembers its name (3.2); `requestNotation` remembers the score's
  names as soon as the file parses (3.2) and sets the `instruments` tag when the opened score

[replaces lines 186-194]
- **`instruments`** is a Sentry tag naming the open score's kinds of instrument, so an issue's
  Tags panel shows when its reports cluster on one instrument. Each kind appears once: `drums` for
  a percussion track (a staff marked percussion, read as `web/lib/alphatab/mixer-tracks.ts`
  already does), otherwise the track's General MIDI program as the engine stores it
  (`playbackInfo.program`, 0–127, counted from 0, so `30` is Distortion Guitar). `drums` comes
  first, then the numbers in ascending order, joined by `,` — `Punk.gp` gives `drums,30`. No name
  table: the engine's own list is internal, and the number is enough. The tag names the score on
  screen, but only once the visitor has opened one: `requestNotation` sets it when the opened
  score replaces the open one. It is never taken from AlphaTab's score-loaded event, which also
  fires for the bundled sample, sometimes after the visitor's file. It is never cleared, so after a
  cancelled or failed open it still names the score that stays on screen. A report of a failed open
  (E101, E102, E103 or E105, the reports with `file`) is sent without it: `reportError` adds
  `instruments: undefined` to that one report's `captureContext` tags. So a failure while opening
  a file never carries the last song's instruments, and a report without the tag comes from a
  failed open or from a visit where the visitor had not opened a file.

What a Drop of F-21 leaves broken: an E105, or an E901 from drawing the new title, that quotes a name from the file being opened reaches Sentry with the name in it.

spike.result: The nested dispatch happened as described: the guard re-rendered the visitor's file inside the sample's event, and the tag handlers saw the visitor's score (nested call) and then the sample (outer call). Final tag: `drums` from the handler that reads the event's argument, `25` from the one that reads `api.score`. `api.score` ended as the visitor's file, TracksPopover's guard returned on the outer call, and AlphaTab's DOM events fired in the order visitor, visitor, sample.

items.corrections: Nothing wrong; three additions. (1) E105 does not always end without a swap: a throw at PlayerShell.tsx:913-923 comes after setNotation, so the new score still replaces the old one. (2) A further way to lose the tag: a second pick during an open is dropped by the one-open-at-a-time guard (:943) after it has cleared the tag. (3) E205 also returns before the swap, but only when the engine failed, so no score is on screen then.
items.notes_for_triage: Option 1 is simpler: one rule in reportError (a report that carries `file` drops the tag), no restore path, and it also covers the dropped second pick. Option 2 needs the still-open score on five paths; OpenFileControl's catch has no api, so report.ts would have to keep the last tag it set, and an E105 thrown after the swap must not put the old tag back. Option 2 also conflicts with F-25's placement (the tag set at the swap): there its catch would restore the old tag over the new score. One related choice neither reviewer raised: an E105 is about the new file, whose instruments are known once it parses; both options send it with no tag, which is the safe reading of the owner's rule. A Drop leaves every report after a cancelled or failed open, for the rest of the visit, without the tag.

evidence: docs.sentry.io/product/issues/issue-details — the issue's tag summary is 'a summary of all tag values for all events included in the issue'; docs.sentry.io/api/events/retrieve-tag-details — a tag's details give `uniqueValues` and `topValues`, each one distinct value with its own `count`. A tag holds one string per event, so `drums,30` and `drums,29,30,33` are separate values.

docs.sentry.io/concepts/search — 'Search supports the wildcard character `*` as a placeholder for specific characters and strings', with `*` shown at the end and at the start. getsentry/sentry:src/sentry/api/event_search.py — translate_wildcard turns `*` anywhere into `.*` in an anchored pattern, and the search bar's 'contains' operator adds `*` at both ends, so `instruments:*030*` is valid. A plain value may hold commas (`value = [^()\t\n ]*`).

Limits: getsentry/relay:relay-event-schema/src/protocol/tags.rs — a key is at most 200 characters from `a-zA-Z0-9_.:-`, a value at most 200 characters with no newline (Sentry's Next.js tags page says the same); getsentry/relay:relay-event-normalization/src/trimming.rs (test_too_long_tags) — a longer value is cut to 200 characters ending in `...`. No limit on the number of tags per event, in the docs or in Relay's event schema.

Fixtures parsed with the installed AlphaTab 1.8.4: web/e2e/fixtures/Punk.gp, Punk.mxl and Punk.alphatex give `drums,30` (`drums,030` padded); guitar-no-percussion.gp, transposed.alphatex and transposed-wide.alphatex give `25` (`025`); the bundled web/public/notation/1-beat.gp and every other fixture give `drums`. No fixture has two programs, so the split across line-ups is reasoned from Sentry's model, not observed.

spike.what: A Node script that parses all 17 fixture and bundled files with the installed AlphaTab and prints the tag in the current format and with 3-digit padding; a count of wildcard over-matches across programs 0–127; a length check against the 200-character value limit.
spike.result: Values as listed above, matching the product-lens reviewer (Punk.gp → drums,30; guitar-no-percussion.gp → 25; the sample → drums). Without padding, 28 of the 128 programs have a `*N*` search that also matches other programs (`*25*` matches 125; `*3*` matches 21 others). With three digits there are none, including across the comma between two numbers. `drums` plus 48 padded programs fits in 200 characters (197); beyond that Relay cuts the value.

- **`instruments`** is a Sentry tag naming the open score's kinds of instrument, so an issue's
  Tags panel shows when its reports cluster on one instrument. Each kind appears once: `drums` for
  a percussion track (a staff marked percussion, read as `web/lib/alphatab/mixer-tracks.ts`
  already does), otherwise the track's General MIDI program as the engine stores it
  (`playbackInfo.program`, 0–127, counted from 0, so `30` is Distortion Guitar). `drums` comes
  first, then the numbers in ascending order, joined by `,` — `Punk.gp` gives `drums,30`. No name
  table: the engine's own list is internal, and the number is enough. The tag is set when a score
  loads, and cleared as soon as another file is picked or dropped, before it is read, so a failure
  while opening it never carries the last song's instruments.

- `tagInstruments`: a percussion track and a Distortion Guitar track (program 30) give
    `drums,30`; two tracks on the same program give one number; an empty list clears the tag;
and it carries the tag `instruments: 25` (the file's one track, an acoustic guitar).

after_draft.text:
- **`instruments`** is a Sentry tag naming the open score's kinds of instrument, so an issue's
  Tags panel shows which sets of instruments its reports came from. Sentry counts each whole value
  as one entry, so `drums,030` and `drums,029,030,033` are two entries; to find every report with
  one instrument, search for its number between wildcards: `instruments:*030*`. Each kind appears
  once: `drums` for a percussion track (a staff marked percussion, read as
  `web/lib/alphatab/mixer-tracks.ts` already does), otherwise the track's General MIDI program as
  the engine stores it (`playbackInfo.program`, 0–127, counted from 0, so `30` is Distortion
  Guitar), written with three digits so that a search for one number never matches another (`25`
  becomes `025`, which `125` does not contain). `drums` comes first, then the numbers in ascending
  order, joined by `,` — `Punk.gp` gives `drums,030`. No name table: the engine's own list is
  internal, and the number is enough. The tag is set when a score loads, and cleared as soon as
  another file is picked or dropped, before it is read, so a failure while opening it never carries
  the last song's instruments.
and it carries the tag `instruments: 025` (the file's one track, an acoustic guitar).

items.scenario: You open an issue in Sentry to check whether its reports come from the acoustic guitar (program 25). The Tags panel lists `25`, `drums,25`, `drums,25,33` and `25,33` as four separate entries, so no single bar stands out. A search for `instruments:*25*` to gather them also returns scores that only use program 125.
items.corrections: PRO-3: the issue page shows a preview of the most common values, but the full list is one click away (the tag details page; the API returns up to 1,000 values), so 'shows only the most common ones' is too strong. ADV-10: 'nothing records which instruments were open during visits that did not fail' is true by design (S2: no counting of attempts), not a defect of this tag.
items.notes_for_triage: A third option was considered: one tag per kind of instrument (for example `instrument.drums` and `instrument.030`, each `yes`). It gives an exact search (`has:instrument.030`) without padding, but the Tags panel shows each key on its own at 100 % `yes`, so it still compares nothing across instruments; it adds one tag per kind to every report, up to 129 keys in the project, and clearing means removing every key set before. Not recommended. F-24 and F-25 edit the same bullet: F-25 makes `drums` mean the visitor's own file, F-24 option 1 changes the format. The combined wording in F-21's notes keeps the bullet as it is up to 'the number is enough.', so option 1's purpose and format sentences replace that part and the combined tail stays. A Drop leaves §2.3 promising a view the panel cannot give.

checks.fix_consistent: Consistent with §3.1 (line 296), §3.4's copy (line 362, 'only the kinds of instrument it uses': 'it' is the visitor's file, which this makes exactly true) and §6 case 4 (a file the visitor opens). It narrows lap 1's ADD-1 ('set on score load') to scores the visitor opened; the owner should confirm. It changes §1 line 103 and §2.3 lines 192-194, and optionally §6 case 1 (484-485).

after_draft.text:
- `web/app/play/OpenFileControl.tsx` and `web/app/play/PlayerShell.tsx`, beyond their catch sites:
  picking or dropping a file remembers its name (3.2) and clears the `instruments` tag (2.3); the
  score-loaded handler remembers the score's names; `requestNotation` sets the tag when an opened
  file replaces the open score, never for the bundled sample; `readNotation` and `LoadedNotation`
  carry the file's extension (2.3).

table: the engine's own list is internal, and the number is enough. The tag is set only from a
  score the visitor opened, when it replaces the open score, never from the bundled sample that
  AlphaTab loads on every visit to `/play`. So `drums` means the visitor's own drum chart, and a
  report without the tag means the visitor had not opened a file of their own, or that an open had
  failed or was still running. The tag is cleared as soon as another file is picked or dropped,
  before it is read, so a failure while opening it never carries the last song's instruments.

1. On `/play`, once the bundled sample is drawn and before any file is opened, a throw the test
       schedules with `setTimeout` inside `page.evaluate` sends an `error` with no `instruments`
       tag. (A direct throw only rejects the `evaluate` call; it never reaches the page.)

items.scenario: You see in Sentry that most reports in an issue carry `instruments: drums`, and you start testing drum charts. In fact most of those visitors never opened a file: AlphaTab loads the bundled one-track beat `1-beat.gp` on every visit to `/play`, and it is tagged `drums` exactly like a visitor's own drum chart.
items.corrections: PRO-5's 'the most common value will probably be drums' is a fair expectation (every visit to /play loads the sample, and many visits may never open a file), but it is not measured.
items.notes_for_triage: The draft sets the tag in requestNotation when an opened file replaces the open score, not in the score-loaded handler. That also closes F-22, and it avoids a stale `notation` in the handler: when NotationSurface's effect fires scoreLoaded, the shell's handler still holds the previous render's state (NotationSurface.tsx:96-102 records the same trap), so a handler that checked `notation` would skip the file just opened. A handler-based version would need a ref written in requestNotation. With F-23 option 1, a report without the tag can also come from a failed open; the draft already says so. A Drop leaves `drums` meaning two different things.

items.scenario: You open a Guitar Pro file whose Notices field holds the transcriber's credit, with their name. A future bug quotes that text in a report that keeps its message, such as an E105. The names filter never learned the Notices field, so the credit reaches Sentry as written.
items.corrections: None; ten is exact for fields. One more piece of file text exists as a getter: `tempoLabel` returns the first tempo marking's text (@coderline/alphatab@1.8.4:dist/alphaTab.core.mjs:3482-3484). Section markers and lyrics are file text too; they are contents rather than names, and §3.1 handles contents by dropping the parse messages.
